chapter: Connie's Inn, Duke Ellington and the Swingland band
title: Improvising on changes rather than melody
summary: Players tried both melody and chord-based improvisation, knowing chord-based playing was inevitable as music grew more complex.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: In your improvisation, were you at that -- or by this time thinking pretty much of just improvising on chord changes or still relating to the melody? It probably varied, I would assume, but --

It varied. Yes. But we tried both, because we wanted all the experience we could get, and I knew that eventually it was gonna come to, you know, the chord deal, so -- There were quite a few guys that came into town, and we used to have the opportunity to listen as these things came about, and we just figured that eventually this was the way it was gonna be.
Do you recall how early that began? I mean, say like going clear back to Connie's Inn or something, how was the improvisation going in those days? That was in the late twenties.
Well, we knew that it was inevitable, because, you know, like -- I hope I'm answering your question right -- as you know, in music there's always a challenge there to try something new.
Right. Become more complex, in a way, more sophisticated.
And we just figured eventually that this was where it was gonna wind up. And it did just that.
